question: As of mid-2026, how many confirmed exoplanets (planets orbiting other stars) have astronomers found?
answer: 6,316 confirmed exoplanets, in 4,725 planetary systems
note: The count keeps climbing steadily as new detection methods and telescopes come online (Wikipedia, NASA Exoplanet Archive data).

question: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about how many times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza?
answer: About 900 times
note: That teaspoon would have a mass of roughly 5.5 trillion kilograms — neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe besides black holes (Wikipedia).

question: Pando, a single aspen tree colony in Utah connected by one shared root system, is considered one of the largest/oldest living organisms on Earth — about how many acres does it cover?
answer: About 106 acres (roughly 43 hectares) — and an estimated 6,000 metric tons
note: Recent habitat modeling suggests it could be up to 16,000 years old, though estimates vary widely (Wikipedia).

question: A single honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) organism discovered in an Oregon forest — one of the largest living organisms ever found — covers about how many acres?
answer: About 2,200 acres (3.5 square miles)
note: Nicknamed the "Humongous Fungus," it's estimated to be around 8,000 years old and could weigh up to 35,000 tons (Wikipedia).

question: What's the fastest non-tornadic surface wind speed ever recorded on Earth?
answer: 408 km/h (253 mph), a gust measured on Barrow Island, Western Australia, during Tropical Cyclone Olivia on 10 April 1996
note: Ratified by the WMO Evaluation Panel in 2010 after confirming the anemometer was sound (Wikipedia).

question: What's the lowest natural air temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth?
answer: −89.2°C (−128.6°F), at Vostok Station, Antarctica, on 21 July 1983
note: Cold enough that exposed skin can get frostbite within minutes (Wikipedia — Vostok Station).

question: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa produced what's considered the loudest sound in recorded history — how far away was it heard?
answer: Up to about 4,800 km (3,000 miles) away, on Rodrigues Island near Mauritius; the pressure wave itself circled the globe more than 3 times
note: Measured at 172-180 decibels from 160 km away — loud enough to rupture sailors' eardrums on ships 64 km from the blast (Wikipedia — 1883 eruption of Krakatoa).

question: The 1958 Lituya Bay event in Alaska produced the tallest wave ever recorded (a "megatsunami") — how tall was it?
answer: 524 metres (1,720 feet) — taller than the Empire State Building — as a landslide dropped about 80 million tons of rock and ice into the bay
note: Triggered by an earthquake on 9 July 1958 (Wikipedia — Megatsunami).

question: Scientists have formally described about 1 million insect species — but how many total insect species are estimated to actually exist on Earth?
answer: As many as 5.5 million species
note: Insects alone may make up around half of all known eukaryote species on the planet (Wikipedia — Insect).

question: A snapping pistol shrimp's claw-clap creates a cavitation bubble that can briefly reach what temperature — nearly as hot as what?
answer: Over 5,000 Kelvin (about 4,700°C) — nearly as hot as the surface of the Sun (about 5,772 K)
note: The snap is also loud enough to stun or kill small prey (Wikipedia — Pistol shrimp).

question: What's the record number of legs found on a single millipede — despite the name meaning "thousand feet"?
answer: 1,306 legs, on a specimen of the species Eumillipes persephone, discovered in Australia
note: More legs than any other creature known on Earth (Wikipedia — Millipede).

question: How long can a sperm whale hold its breath on its longest recorded dives?
answer: Up to about 120 minutes (2 hours), diving as deep as 2,250 metres (7,380 feet)
note: Made possible by a flexible ribcage, huge oxygen-storing myoglobin reserves, and extra-rich blood (Wikipedia — Sperm whale).

question: A female ocean sunfish (Mola mola) can release how many eggs at once — more than any other known vertebrate?
answer: Up to 300 million eggs at a time
note: Despite this, only a tiny fraction ever survive to adulthood (Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish).

question: In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania, setting a world record. How far did it fly without stopping once?
answer: 13,560 km (8,435 miles), over 11 days and 1 hour, without landing to rest, eat, or drink
note: The bird, tagged "B6," beat the previous nonstop-flight record (Wikipedia — Bar-tailed godwit).

question: How fast can the fastest-growing bamboo species grow in a single day, under ideal conditions?
answer: Up to about 91 cm (36 inches) in 24 hours — roughly 40 mm (1.5 inches) every hour, fast enough to visibly move
note: Guinness World Record; some individual shoots of Japanese giant timber bamboo have been observed growing up to 120 cm (47 in) in a day (Wikipedia — Bamboo).

question: About how many galaxies does the observable universe contain, according to current estimates?
answer: As many as an estimated 2 trillion galaxies (though some more conservative estimates put it in the hundreds of billions)
note: The observable universe itself spans about 93 billion light-years across (Wikipedia — Observable universe).

question: Bacteria cells living in and on the human body roughly match human cells in number — about how many bacteria cells does an average human body host?
answer: An estimated 38 trillion bacteria cells, versus roughly 30-40 trillion human cells — close to a 1:1 ratio
note: This overturned the old "10-to-1" bacteria-to-human-cell myth that circulated for decades (Wikipedia — Human microbiome).

question: What's the longest single lightning flash ("megaflash") ever recorded, measured by distance?
answer: 829 km (515 miles) — a single bolt that stretched across Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Kansas, and Mississippi in October 2017
note: Detected retrospectively via satellite data and confirmed as a world record in 2025 (Wikipedia — Lightning).

question: What's the fastest speed ever reached by a human-made object — NASA's Parker Solar Probe, during its closest pass by the Sun?
answer: About 690,000 km/h (430,000 mph), or roughly 191 km per second
note: Reached in December 2024; at that speed you could cross the continental US in under 30 seconds (Wikipedia — Parker Solar Probe).

question: What's the deepest known cave on Earth, and how deep does it go?
answer: Krubera Cave in Georgia (the country), reaching 2,224 metres (7,297 feet) deep
note: Depth confirmed via a 2024 resurvey and dive at the bottom sump — deep enough to swallow more than seven Eiffel Towers stacked on top of each other (Wikipedia — Krubera Cave).

question: Rafflesia arnoldii produces the largest single flower of any plant on Earth — how wide and how heavy can one bloom get?
answer: Over 100 cm (about 40 inches) across — one record specimen measured 111 cm — and weighing up to 10 kg (22 lb)
note: It's also famous for smelling like rotting meat to attract carrion flies (Wikipedia — Rafflesia).

question: A star-nosed mole has 22 tentacles on its nose and is famous for eating incredibly fast — what's the record time from touching a piece of food to swallowing it?
answer: As little as 120 milliseconds (its brain decides whether something is edible in about 8 milliseconds — one of the fastest reactions in the animal kingdom)
note: Average time is 227 milliseconds; the mole is effectively blind and hunts entirely by touch (Wikipedia — Star-nosed mole).

question: Sharks have been evolving for hundreds of millions of years — about how many distinct species of shark are known today?
answer: More than 500 species, spread across 13 different orders
note: They range from the 17 cm dwarf lanternshark to the whale shark, which can exceed 12 metres (Wikipedia — Shark).

question: What is the heaviest heart ever recorded in any animal, belonging to a stranded blue whale?
answer: 180 kg (about 400 lb) — roughly the weight of a baby grand piano
note: Measured from a stranded North Atlantic blue whale; it's the largest known heart of any animal, living or extinct (Wikipedia — Blue whale).

question: Gray whales make the longest annual migration of any mammal on Earth — how far is the round trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican breeding lagoons?
answer: Between 16,000 and 22,000 km (9,900-13,700 miles) round trip
note: They average about 120 km (75 miles) a day at roughly 8 km/h (5 mph) (Wikipedia — Gray whale).

question: What's the largest iceberg ever recorded — bigger than an entire European country?
answer: An Antarctic tabular iceberg spotted in 1956, measuring 335 by 97 km (208 by 60 miles) — larger than the entire country of Belgium
note: Sighted by the USS Glacier on 12 November 1956 in the South Pacific (Wikipedia — Iceberg).

question: How tall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, the world's tallest waterfall?
answer: 979 metres (3,212 ft) total height, including a single uninterrupted plunge of 807 metres (2,648 ft) — nearly 20 times taller than Niagara Falls
note: Water falls so far that much of it evaporates into mist before reaching the bottom (Wikipedia — Angel Falls).

question: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the world's deepest lake — how deep does it go, and what share of the planet's unfrozen fresh water does it hold?
answer: 1,642 metres (5,387 ft) deep, holding about 19% of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth
note: That's more fresh water than all five of North America's Great Lakes combined (Wikipedia — Lake Baikal).

question: Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system in the world — how many miles of passageways have been mapped so far?
answer: More than 426 miles (686 km) surveyed as of 2025 — and explorers keep finding more
note: The next-longest known cave system in the world is barely a quarter of that length (Wikipedia — Mammoth Cave National Park).

question: How big can the General Sherman Tree in California get — the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth by volume?
answer: About 1,487 cubic metres (52,500 cubic feet) of wood, standing 83.8 m (275 ft) tall with a base 11.1 m (36.5 ft) across
note: It's neither the tallest nor the widest nor the oldest tree species — just the biggest by sheer volume (Wikipedia — General Sherman (tree)).

question: What's the heaviest capybara ever recorded — the world's largest living rodent?
answer: 91 kg (201 lb), a wild female found in Brazil
note: That's roughly the size of an adult human, for an animal in the same family as guinea pigs (Wikipedia — Capybara).

question: In 2021, scientists sequenced the oldest DNA ever recovered, from mammoth teeth found frozen in Siberia. How old was it?
answer: Up to 1.65 million years old — more than a million years older than any previously sequenced DNA
note: It revealed a previously unknown mammoth lineage, from teeth found at Krestovka, eastern Siberia (Wikipedia — Woolly mammoth).

question: How long can totality last during the longest possible total lunar eclipse?
answer: Up to about 107 minutes — well under 2 hours, though the entire eclipse event (partial phases included) can stretch up to nearly 4 hours (236 minutes)
note: Compare to a total solar eclipse, whose totality maxes out at just 7.5 minutes (Wikipedia — Lunar eclipse).

question: Monarch butterflies migrate every year from the northeastern US and Canada to central Mexico — how far can that single journey be?
answer: Between 1,200 and 2,800 miles (or more)
note: No single butterfly makes the round trip — it takes multiple generations, none of which have ever flown the route before (Wikipedia — Monarch butterfly).

question: How much did the largest colossal squid ever recorded weigh?
answer: 495 kg (1,091 lb) — caught in the Ross Sea off Antarctica in 2007, now on display in New Zealand
note: It's the heaviest cephalopod (squid/octopus relative) ever recorded, though some beaks found in sperm whale stomachs suggest even bigger ones may exist (Wikipedia — Colossal squid).

question: What's the deepest a human has ever dived underwater unassisted by breathing equipment (the "no-limits" freediving world record)?
